_README: THE SUBSTRATE, AS STAGES THE OWNER CAN FOLLOW. Rendered by GUI tab 9 (SUBSTRATE).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS RATHER THAN PROSE IN THE GUI: a panel of hardcoded sentences rots
silently. Every row here carries `reviewed_utc`, and the GUI shows a row's age and turns it
AMBER past 3 days / RED past 7. A maintained tab that cannot show its own staleness is a
promise; one that can is a control.
RULES FOR EDITING, WHICH THE VALIDATOR ENFORCES (tools/substrate_progress.py --check):
1. `evidence` states a NUMBER and `floor` states what it must beat. A number with no floor
is not evidence -- that is this repo's oldest rule and the validator refuses the row.
2. `source` must be a path that EXISTS on disk. A citation nobody can open is a claim.
3. `state` is one of WORKS / WEAK / BROKEN / UNTESTED / UNKNOWN. There is no 'good'.
4. `plain` must avoid metric, organ and arm names -- the owner has asked four times.
5. Update `reviewed_utc` ONLY when the row was actually re-checked, never as a refresh.
This is 10 stages, not 159 modules and not 40 organs. The module-level view is ORGAN_MAP.md.
This is the view that answers 'are we on track and what is in the way'.

2026-08-24: `problem` (single string) became `problems` (list). A stage is worked by SEVERAL briefs, and the single field made 8 of 10 stages read as unowned while 20 briefs existed -- a false 'nobody is working this' shipped to the GUI header.

headline.the_wall: The step that decides what words mean learns the WRONG RELATION -- which words appear together, not which words are interchangeable -- and every unsupervised fix we have tried misses information we can prove is there.
headline.plain: The system reads text, files what it finds, keeps it, and can be asked about it -- that whole path works. The step in the middle that decides what a word MEANS does not, and 2026-08-23 made it precise: it is not weak, it is backwards. It scores 0.051 where guessing scores 0.486 and a right answer scores 0.960, because it confidently treats words that turn up together as words that mean the same thing. Three separate tests now agree on where the remaining hope is: whenever an oracle is allowed to pick the best source per question, it beats everything we have -- so the knowledge is present and what is missing is knowing which of our own sources to trust. Every one of those oracles is allowed to see the answers, and a child is not, which is the open question on the board.
headline.why_it_matters: Nine of the ten stages below can be improved without changing the answer to 'can this thing understand what it read'. Stage 2 is the one that decides it -- and two results on 2026-08-23 pointed at it from stages 1 and 4 independently.

stages.name: READ THE TEXT
stages.plain: Take ordinary prose and pull out what happened to things -- which substance dissolved, which object moved.
stages.evidence: 90 of 100 hand-checked correct, against a trivial method's 70.5 on the same items (difference +0.23, 95% CI +0.13 to +0.33)
stages.floor: RUN 2026-08-23. Strongest trivial method scores 0.7053 and the real one beats it with the interval excluding zero. An information-free twin scores 0.09, so the comparison can tell things apart.
stages.gap: THE FLOOR PASSED AND A SHARPER TEST DID NOT. A two-line rule using only word order and active/passive voice -- with all six filters removed -- reaches 0.83, and the real method beats THAT by somewhere between 0.00 and 0.14, which does not exclude zero. So most of the 90% is the filters plus two lines of code, not the elaborate reading.
stages.goal: Stop improving the filters. Either show the elaborate reading beats the two-line rule at power, or replace it with the two-line rule and spend the effort on stage 2.

stages.name: DECIDE WHAT WORDS MEAN
stages.plain: Work out what a newly-read word means by relating it to words already understood.
stages.evidence: On the test of whether two words are INTERCHANGEABLE, our own rule scores 0.051 where pure guessing scores 0.486 and a right answer scores 0.960. It is not weak, it is BACKWARDS -- it confidently calls words similar when they merely turn up together. Counting which words co-occur beats our whole apparatus 2-3x on assigning meanings (0.048-0.065 vs 0.016-0.030, three runs).
stages.floor: Guessing scores 0.486 on the interchangeability test and a correct answer 0.960; we read 0.051. On meaning-assignment we beat a random answer on 2 of 3 runs but lose to plain co-occurrence counting on 3 of 3. The sensory ratings score 0.599 there, but a control giving EVERY WORD THE SAME VECTOR scores 0.619 and beats them.
stages.gap: THE CENTRAL DEFECT, AND IT IS NOW SHARPER THAN 'WEAK'. The step learns the WRONG RELATION -- which words appear together, not which words are interchangeable -- and it learns it confidently. Two pre-registered stop conditions have now closed the whole family of fixes that reshuffle word-co-occurrence counts: four tuning variants moved it from 0.052 to 0.114 and no further. The sensory ratings do not rescue it either: they point the right way but do not beat a control carrying no word-specific information at all.
stages.goal: CHANGED 2026-08-23, AND THE PREVIOUS GOAL IS NOW KNOWN TO BE INSUFFICIENT. It said 'wire in the human sensory ratings'. Measured on this test, those ratings do not beat a no-information control, so wiring them in would not fix the step. What the evidence points to instead: a method that is allowed to see answers reaches 0.960 on data it has never seen, so the information IS in the text and no unsupervised route we have tried reaches it. The open question -- where a learning signal comes from without being handed answers -- is on the board as Q118 and is a research question, not a sweep.

stages.name: DECIDE WHAT TO KEEP
stages.plain: Judge which of the things just read are solid enough to file, and throw the rest away.
stages.evidence: Accepts 68 of 555 candidates (12.3%); knowledge grows as 8.4 x sentences^0.473
stages.floor: Must not be near 0% (accepts nothing) or near 100% (accepts anything). 12.3% is a real filter. Growth exponent below 1.0 is the expected shape for vocabulary growth.
stages.gap: None known. Tested under nested sampling at several reading volumes: it never lost knowledge it already had, in 12 of 12 samples.
stages.goal: Leave it alone. This stage is not the bottleneck and re-tuning it would be motion without progress.

stages.name: KEEP IT BETWEEN RUNS
stages.plain: Remember what was learned last time instead of starting from nothing every run.
stages.evidence: Wired 2026-08-23. A resumed start carries 390 facts against a cold start's 92, and keeps its place in the consolidation schedule.
stages.floor: A cold start must be unchanged by the wiring -- verified byte-identical at 92 facts. An off-arm proves the loading is real rather than asserted.
stages.gap: It does NOT do what we hoped. A measurement landed with the wiring: resuming makes a fresh read ground almost nothing new (9 versus 168), because genuinely new words fail to match anything in the saved memory. Correctness is at chance either way.
stages.goal: Keep it for accumulation -- a system that discards its store every run has no long-term memory at all. Do NOT bill it as a fix for stage 2. That prediction is retired.

stages.name: GET IT BACK OUT
stages.plain: Answer a question by finding the right thing among everything filed.
stages.evidence: Ask with the exact words it stored and it answers 0.912. Ask with only some of them, which is all real reading gives, and it answers 0.162. Six different memory designs were built and the best reached 0.246, against plain word-counting at 0.324.
stages.floor: Plain first-order word-counting scores 0.324 and no memory design beat it; the best reached 0.246, a shortfall whose interval excludes zero. Scrambled and information-free versions score 0.000-0.0002, and a self-retrieval check scores 0.977, so the test works.
stages.gap: The store can RECITE but not RECOGNISE. Crucially this is NOT a storage-format problem: word-counting already IS the same kind of signal our elaborate store was trying to be, which is why it keeps winning. But an oracle allowed to pick the best source per question scores 0.408 and BEATS counting by a margin whose interval excludes zero -- so there is real unused signal here that no automatic method reaches.
stages.goal: Stop redesigning the store; that route is closed on three separate tests. Build the thing that decides WHICH source to trust for THIS question. The same missing piece shows up independently in the meaning step, so it is one component, not two.

stages.name: SAY "I DON'T KNOW"
stages.plain: Refuse to answer when the evidence is not there, instead of guessing.
stages.evidence: Refusing to answer about made-up words works almost perfectly: it accepts real words it has read 1.000 of the time and rejects invented strings 0.999. But that test is easier than it looks, because the real words were exactly the words already in memory.
stages.floor: A gate refusing the same share at random scores 0.500; this scores 0.999. The approach originally proposed -- refusing when the answer looks uncertain -- scores 0.568 and 0.524, which sits AT that 0.500 floor and does not work.
stages.gap: Measured 2026-08-23, the arm nobody had run: on ordinary English words it simply has not read, the same gate refuses 85.8% of them, including everyday words like abdomen and abduct. Only about an eighth of that is word-endings it should have recognised; the rest is vocabulary it genuinely has never seen. And the figure is not fixed -- it refuses 94.9% after 800 sentences and 85.8% after 5,200, still improving.
stages.goal: Ship it switched OFF by default, or on only where refusing unfamiliar words is what you want. Refusing a word you have never met is arguably correct behaviour, but nobody should read the near-perfect score as the system knowing what it knows about English. It knows what it has read.

stages.name: KNOW WHAT IT IS MISSING
stages.plain: Notice which piece of knowledge would most help, so reading can be aimed rather than random.
stages.evidence: Aimed reading DID beat reading random text: it grounded 6.2 words per 100 held-out against 1.3 for random, a 3.9x gain, over a 10,000-sentence read. But on that same measure the OLD fixed reading schedule scored 7.4 -- BETTER than aiming. And on agreement with a dictionary, random reading (0.386) beat aimed reading (0.351).
stages.floor: It cleared the floor it declared -- beat random by at least 10% relative, and it beat it by 287%. It was never required to beat the fixed schedule, and on the headline coverage measure it does not: 6.2 against 7.4 per 100.
stages.gap: THE ORGAN IS BUILT AND THE LIVE READER DOES NOT CALL IT. hdlab/information_foraging.py exists, is witnessed, is registered as wired, and its brain rule is properly pinned (Charnov's marginal-value theorem). What actually reads is still a hard-coded list of four sources. Separately, the one run that tested it has a known 7.6x bias in which kind of text the test words came from, and it did not save the words it scored, so that cannot be corrected without re-running about 70 minutes per arm.
stages.goal: Two things, and neither is a build. Give the live reader a call site so aiming actually happens during reading. Then re-run the comparison with the bias controlled and the scored words saved, and require it to beat the FIXED schedule rather than only random -- because on today's numbers it loses to the fixed schedule on the measure that matters.
stages.state_note: CORRECTION, NOT PROGRESS (2026-08-24). This stage read UNTESTED with a floor of 'Not run'. Both were wrong: exp_information_foraging_reading_v1 ran a full 10,000-sentence read and HARD_PASSed its declared bands. The substrate did not change; my label did.

stages.name: REASON OVER WHAT IT KNOWS
stages.plain: Combine several stored facts to answer something never read directly.
stages.evidence: Reasoning components are built and registered; no end-to-end measurement on the current store
stages.floor: Must beat answering from the question's surface wording, and from the single most similar stored fact.
stages.gap: Not the current bottleneck. Reasoning over facts whose meanings are at chance (stage 2) would measure the reasoner against corrupted inputs, and a null would not tell us which stage failed.
stages.goal: Hold until stage 2 moves. Testing this first would waste a clean measurement on a known-bad input.

stages.name: PROVE A RESULT IS REAL
stages.plain: Re-run a past result from scratch and get the same answer, rather than replaying saved output.
stages.evidence: 5 of 5 solved problems reproduced; 71.2% of 4,908 landed results (3,495) can be genuinely re-run today
stages.floor: A re-run must be able to FAIL. Proven by breaking an input on purpose and watching the verdict flip, then restoring it. And the redirect itself is positive-controlled in a fresh process, so 'it works' is not an assumption.
stages.gap: 1,413 results still replay a saved answer instead of recomputing. Of those, 425 assert a result and 135 of THOSE are quoted by something that steers our work -- that is the list worth spending re-runs on.
stages.goal: Done for new work: a commit adding an experiment that writes a result is now refused unless it can be re-run. Remaining: work the 135 cited-and-unverifiable results one at a time, as the owner asked.

stages.name: KEEP WHAT WE GAIN
stages.plain: Make sure a working improvement gets connected into the system instead of stranded in an experiment.
stages.evidence: 212 registered capabilities; 0 unregistered modules; 41 of 42 shelved items name what would revive them
stages.floor: The check must be able to fire. Positive-controlled -- a deliberately blank entry is caught.
stages.gap: None material. An earlier claim here that the shelf was 'hollow' was my own error, retracted the same day: I measured a field named nearly-right while the correct one sat filled beside it.
stages.goal: Leave it alone. It is doing its job.
